opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's quite a significant mismatch there, actually. Most of the standard benchmarks are essentially single-shot affairs. You pose a question, maybe a maths problem or a coding task or a multiple-choice item, the model produces an answer, and you score it. That tells you something useful about raw capability, but it's a very thin slice of how people actually engage with these systems.

In practice, a lot of people are having long, meandering conversations with these models, sometimes stretching over hours, or returning to them over days. And in that setting, what matters is rather different. It's not just whether the model gets a particular answer right. It's whether it stays coherent, whether it keeps track of what's been said, whether it maintains a consistent persona, and whether it drifts. That last one is particularly interesting to me.

I've often found it helpful to think of these models as role-playing, as engaged in a kind of improvised performance. At the start of a conversation, the system prompt and the first few exchanges establish a character, and the model plays that character. But over a long conversation, the character can shift. The model is always conditioning on everything that has come before, so if the conversation wanders into strange territory, the character it's playing can wander with it. You get these phenomena where a model that was perfectly well-behaved in turn three is saying something quite odd in turn two hundred. No single-turn benchmark is going to capture that, because the behaviour simply isn't present in the first few turns.

There's also a more subtle issue, which is that in a long conversation the user and the model are co-constructing something together. The user's expectations, the way they frame things, even their emotional state, all feed back into what the model produces. So evaluation becomes much harder, because you're no longer measuring a property of the model in isolation. You're measuring a property of a dynamical system that includes a human being.

So I'd say standard evaluations are necessary but nowhere near sufficient. We need ways of assessing consistency, stability of character, and the trajectories conversations tend to follow, not just the quality of individual responses. And frankly, that's a much more difficult and much more interesting problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts single-shot benchmarks with how people actually use models in long, meandering conversations, explicitly calling this a significant mismatch.

r002.rationale: It says the user and model co-construct the interaction and that the user’s expectations, framing, and emotional state feed back into the model’s responses, while the character can shift over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's a fairly significant mismatch, actually. The standard benchmarks, by and large, present the model with a question or a task, the model produces an answer, and you score it. It's essentially a snapshot. A single turn, or a handful of turns at most, with a well-defined target.

But that's not really how most people interact with these systems. People have long, meandering conversations. They come back to earlier threads, they change their minds, they introduce ambiguities, sometimes deliberately, sometimes not. And the character of the exchange evolves over time. The model is, in a sense, building up a kind of context, a kind of shared history, and what it produces at turn fifty depends on everything that's happened before, not just on the immediate question.

So the evaluations are measuring something, and it's not nothing. They tell you about the model's competence at particular kinds of tasks. But I don't think they tell you very much about what it's like to actually live with one of these things, if I can put it that way. They don't capture the ways the model might drift, or become sycophantic, or lose track of what was agreed earlier, or indeed the ways it might become increasingly impressive as the context fills up with useful material.

And there's a conceptual point here too, which I think is worth dwelling on. We tend to talk about "the model" as if it's a fixed entity with fixed properties, and the benchmark reveals those properties. But what you're really dealing with in a long conversation is something more like a role-play that's unfolding. The model is, as it were, generating a character, and that character is shaped by the whole conversation. So asking "how good is the model" is a bit like asking how good an actor is without specifying the play. The benchmark gives you one very particular, rather artificial play.

So I'd want to see much more work on evaluations that are longitudinal, that look at the dynamics of extended interaction, and that are honest about the fact that a lot of what matters to users is not really reducible to a number on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts snapshot, single-turn benchmarks with the extended, evolving conversations people have with models.

r002.rationale: It says the model generates a character shaped by the whole conversation, which communicates that users shape the interaction's character over time.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s a gap there. A standard evaluation typically gives the model a question, gets an answer, and scores it. That can tell us something useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us what happens when somebody engages with the model over a long conversation.

In a conversation, each response becomes part of the context for the next one. The user might challenge an answer, introduce an assumption, or gradually draw the model into a particular way of talking. So what you’re observing is an unfolding interaction, and the quality of that interaction isn’t captured simply by whether the model got the first answer right.

For example, if you challenge a correct answer, does the model defend it appropriately, or does it agree with you? If it makes a mistake, can it recover? Those are things we ought to evaluate as well. I wouldn’t say the standard benchmarks are useless, but we should be careful about extrapolating from them to the experience of using these systems over many turns.

r001.rationale: It contrasts evaluations that score a single question and answer with what happens in extended, multi-turn conversations.

r002.rationale: It says users can introduce assumptions and gradually draw the model into a particular way of talking, showing how they shape the interaction over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s quite a gap between the two. A standard evaluation typically presents the model with a question and scores its answer. That’s useful, but it captures a rather narrow slice of what happens when somebody engages with a model over a long conversation.

In a conversation, each response changes the context for what comes next. The user adapts to the model, the model responds to that adaptation, and you can end up somewhere that you wouldn’t have anticipated from looking at individual questions and answers. A mistaken assumption, for example, might get corrected, or it might become embedded in the conversation and elaborated upon.

So I’d want to evaluate the interaction as well as the individual response. Can the model recover from a misunderstanding? Does it maintain an appropriate degree of uncertainty? What happens when the user repeatedly pushes it towards a particular view? Those are properties of a trajectory through a conversation, and they’re much harder to capture with a single benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts evaluations that score a model’s answer to a single question with the narrower coverage they provide of extended conversations.

r002.rationale: It says users adapt to the model and can repeatedly push it toward a particular view, shaping how the conversation develops over time.
